seoDescription: Learn about JavaScript Signals, a powerful concept for managing reactive variables that is revolutionizing modern frameworks and is now proposed for native implementation. This explanation covers the core ideas behind signals, including how they track state changes over time and automatically update the UI. Understand key related concepts like computed state for derived values and effects for running side-effects.

chapters.description: The hosts introduce the topic of JavaScript Signals, a concept being implemented in all major frameworks and now has an early-stage proposal for native JavaScript.

chapters.description: The hosts engage in some lighthearted banter about old band t-shirts before presenting a message from the sponsor, Sentry.

chapters.title: What Are Signals? The Core Concept
chapters.description: This chapter defines signals as reactive variables that allow you to react to data changes, such as updating the DOM or computing new values.

chapters.title: Understanding Effects and Computed State
chapters.description: The discussion covers effects (side effects) for running code when a signal changes and introduces computed state as the preferred way to create new state derived from existing signals.

chapters.title: Signals vs. React's Top-Down State
chapters.description: This segment contrasts the flexibility of signals, which can be updated from anywhere, with React's unidirectional, top-down state management model.

chapters.title: How Signals Update the DOM
chapters.description: This chapter explains how frameworks like SolidJS and Svelte use signals to directly update specific parts of the DOM, bypassing the need for a virtual DOM.

chapters.title: The Future: Native Browser Implementation
chapters.description: The hosts discuss the exciting future prospect of signals and reactive templates being implemented natively in the browser, which would lead to lighter and more performant frameworks.

chapters.title: Practical Implementations: Preact Signals
chapters.description: An overview of the Preact Signals library, covering its core API functions like signal, computed, effect, and the performance-enhancing batch function.

chapters.title: The Elegance of Preact Signals Code
chapters.description: Wes expresses his admiration for the Preact Signals library, highlighting its lightweight nature and clever implementation that automatically tracks dependencies without a dependency array.

chapters.title: Other Frameworks: SolidJS and the Origins in KnockoutJS
chapters.description: This chapter credits SolidJS for popularizing modern signals and takes a look back at KnockoutJS from 2010, which pioneered many of these reactive concepts.

chapters.title: The Future of the JavaScript Signals Proposal
chapters.description: A look at the current status of the native JavaScript signals proposal, noting it is a major browser primitive that will take time to get right.

chapters.title: Conclusion
chapters.description: The hosts conclude by affirming that signals are becoming a standard way of thinking about state and give a final shout-out to the pioneers of the concept.

summary:
## What are JavaScript Signals?

Signals are a system for creating **reactive variables** in JavaScript. They represent a piece of state that may change over time. When a signal's value changes, any dependent code automatically runs to react to that change.

This is useful for many common web development tasks:
- Updating the UI to display the new value.
- Re-calculating derived data (e.g., a shopping cart total).
- Triggering side effects (e.g., sending data to a server).

## Core Primitives of a Signal System

Most signal implementations, like **Preact Signals**, provide a few core functions:

- **`signal(initialValue)`**: Creates a new signal, which is a container for a value that can change.
- **`computed(() => ...)`**: Creates a new signal whose value is derived from other signals. It automatically re-calculates whenever its dependencies change.
- **`effect(() => ...)`**: Runs a function and automatically re-runs it whenever the signals used inside it change. This is used for side effects like updating the DOM.
- **`batch(() => ...)`**: Groups multiple signal updates together into a single, atomic change, which can improve performance by preventing multiple unnecessary re-renders.

> [!TIP]
> When one piece of state depends on another, it's better to use **computed state** (sometimes called `derived`) rather than writing an `effect` that manually updates a second signal. This ensures the relationship is clear and managed automatically.

## Signals vs. Traditional Framework State

A key difference between signals and the state model in a framework like **React** is how updates propagate.

- **React State**: Is generally **unidirectional and top-down**. State and update functions must be passed down through props, which can lead to prop-drilling and cause entire component subtrees to re-render.
- **Signals**: Are not tied to a component hierarchy. They can be created and updated from anywhere in the application. Updates are granular, meaning only the specific parts of the DOM that depend on a signal are changed, without needing a Virtual DOM or re-rendering entire components.

## Implementations and the Future

Many modern frameworks are built around signals:
- **SolidJS**: Widely credited with popularizing the modern implementation of signals.
- **Svelte (Runes)**: The latest version of Svelte adopts signals as its core reactive primitive.
- **Qwik, Vue, Angular**: All have their own implementations of signals.
- **Preact Signals**: A lightweight, framework-agnostic library that can be used in React, vanilla JS, or anywhere else.
- **KnockoutJS (2010)**: An early pioneer of many of these reactive, observable-based concepts.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> There is a **TC39 proposal to add signals to JavaScript natively**. It is currently at Stage 1, meaning it is still in the early exploration phase. Because it's a major browser primitive, it will likely take time to be standardized, but frameworks are building their APIs in a way that will allow them to adopt the native version seamlessly in the future.

This native implementation promises to make frameworks lighter, more memory-efficient, and faster.
